newsitem.title: USA: News Corp finds book publishing perilous.
newsitem.headline: News Corp finds book publishing perilous.

text.p: By announcing a huge US$270 million charge at its HarperCollins unit Monday, News Corp has acknowledged its foray into book publishing has been fraught with financial peril, analysts and industry executives said.
"That's a fairly significant writedown," said Chris Dixon, an analyst at PaineWebber. "It's going to take three years to recover that writedown, if you use 1996 annual cash flow of $71 million."
"The reality is News Corp recognizes this year is going to be a little more trying than they originally hoped," Dixon said. "There are clearly a number of problems at HarperCollins."

News Corp said its 1997 year results would include an extraordinary charge of US$270 million related to the restructuring. It said the charge comes after the company completed a year-long restructuring at the book publisher.
A spokesman said the writeoff would be a mixture of cancelling and buying out author contracts as well as book inventory writedowns.
News Corp said a total of 420 persons were being laid off from HarperCollins. About 220 jobs have already been cut, and another 200 will still be slashed, including 40 in the U.S.
The New York Times reported earlier this year that the publisher was cancelling dozens of author contracts, especially for fiction that was not considered commercial.
Publishing executives said the announcement could pose a new set of problems for HarperCollins.
They said some agents may choose to keep their authors away from HarperCollins if they feel the publisher is beleaguered.
"They will have two problems," said one publishing executive, who declined to be identified. "Attracting new authors and new material from agents, and keeping the authors they have."
Some analysts estimated that total book publishing revenues for this year will be abut $785 million, with estimated cash flow of $34 million.

Industry executives have noted that the publisher has gone through its author lists and "cleaned out" those deemed unprofitable. HarperCollins, like virtually all publishers, have suffered some deep-rooted industry problems, including the financial burden of accepting returns of unsold books from booksellers.
The executive said: "Perhaps they feel they can't find a buyer, so they have no recourse but to go forward."
News Corp said it has no plans to sell its HarperCollins book publishing unit. In a statement, the company said it is "reaffirming its long-term commitment to the business."
"It's a brave announcement," said the executive. "The question is was it made out of necessity, or a deeply held belief to persevere in the business."
